Subject: Dedicated GPU reservation — queueing behavior & SLA draft

Hi Evan / Priya,

Attached is the first pass of the Dedicated capacity SLA we've discussed for Genemind. The draft reflects the reserved 8-GPU pool we scoped during the Q4 sizing call and includes throughput and uptime targets we typically offer for Dedicated customers.

Key items in the draft (high level):
- Reserved capacity: 8x A100-equivalent GPUs dedicated to your deployment
- Baseline throughput: 4,000 tokens/sec sustained across the pool (excl. IO variance)
- Uptime target: 99.9% monthly availability (excludes scheduled maintenance windows)
- Latency SLOs: p95 < 400ms for model footprints <= 1024 tokens; p99 < 1.2s
- Queueing & throttling: local per-instance queue with max 250 concurrent requests; backpressure and 429 on sustained overload; burst buffer for 30s at 2x baseline
- Exception process: requests for SLA exceptions (e.g., extended maintenance or capacity pauses) handled via a formal change request with calendar and rollback plan

Please review the attached PDF and the latency CSV (benchmarks from our staging run). Two open questions for you: 1) Do you need a guaranteed global burst window larger than 30s for nightly batch runs? 2) Will any of your teams require hard p99 guarantees for >= 2048 token responses?

If helpful, Marcus and Aditya are copied to jump in on technical/contract details.

Thanks,
Neha Kapoor

Thanks for the draft. A few quick notes from our infra team after a first pass of the benchmarks: we expect two peak patterns over the next 12 months — (A) steady low-latency online inference (bursty but small payloads) and (B) nightly model refresh scoring jobs that send large batches for evaluation.

Questions / requests:
1) For pattern B, can we request an SLA exception that allows a scheduled 2-hour window once per week where we can push sustained throughput to 2x baseline without 429s? We understand this impacts shared capacity planning but need it for nightly scoring.
2) For pattern A, in production we need p99 closer to 900ms for responses up to 1024 tokens. Is that achievable with the reserved 8 GPUs?
3) How does Redwood handle queue aging — do older requests get dropped after a TTL? We'd prefer a predictable behavior (either FIFO with TTL or priority lanes for control traffic).

If you can share an explicit queueing/overload policy and the exception process, we can present to our SRE and procurement teams next week.

Hi all,

Following up with the technical details you asked for. I ran a targeted set of staging runs last month with Genemind model artifacts (thanks for providing checkpoints) and validated the data in latency-benchmark-12-2025.csv. Below are the operational policies and a proposal for the exception window.

Summary of operational behavior (proposed formal text for SLA appendix):
1) Queueing model
   - Per-node request queue: FIFO, max outstanding requests = 250 per serving instance.
   - Request TTL: 90 seconds. Requests exceeding TTL are rejected with a 410 if already dequeued or 429 if still queued when the TTL expires.
   - Priority lanes: control plane (health checks, management calls) use a separate small lane and are never evicted by user traffic. No per-customer priority lanes by default on Dedicated.
2) Burst behavior & weekly exception
   - Burst buffer: load balancer maintains a 30-second soft burst at up to 2x baseline throughput (no SLA credit during burst).
   - Weekly scheduled exception: we can grant Genemind a recurring 2-hour weekly window (time agreed in contract) during which the carrier will raise the burst cap to 2x sustained throughput for the reserved pool and suppress queue TTL evictions (i.e., fewer 429s) provided the activity happens only inside the window.
   - Operational constraints: exception window must be scheduled, communicated 72 hours in advance for planned scale-ups exceeding 2x baseline, and Redwood retains right to pause exceptions for emergency maintenance with 4-hour notice.
3) Latency & throughput guarantees (for 8x A100-equivalent GPUs)
   - Sustained throughput guarantee: 4,000 tokens/sec across the pool measured as rolling 5-min average.
   - Latency SLOs (responses <= 1024 tokens): p95 < 400ms, p99 < 950ms on 90% of deployment days. The p99 figure here reflects staging runs with typical request size distribution; real-world variance from customer input distribution can impact tail latency.
   - For responses >1024 tokens or for the 7B variant under heavy memory pressure, p99 can increase to ~1.2s; those cases should be enumerated in the appendix as usage patterns that may require a higher GPU count or different quantization profile.
4) Failure & credit policy
   - Uptime definition: service endpoint availability measured at the platform ingress for the reserved pool. Scheduled maintenance windows (announced >=72 hours) are excluded from uptime calculations.
   - SLA credit bands: monthly availability >= 99.9% = no credits; 99.0–99.9% = 10% monthly credit; <99.0% = escalation and review for 25% credit. Credits are prorated against Dedicated fees.
   - For exceptions resulting from contractor misuse or customer-caused noisy neighbor behavior, credits are not issued.

Operational recommendation for Genemind:
- If you require p99 ~900ms consistently for 1024-token responses, we recommend upgrading to a 12-GPU reserved pool or enabling an additional burst buffer (non-SLA) for your nightly job windows. The weekly 2-hour exception is possible but should be combined with a short-term horizontal scale-up for predictable tail performance.

Next steps:
- Neha: share the revised SLA PDF with the weekly exception text and the formal appendix wording above.
- Evan / Priya: confirm whether the weekly 2-hour window is acceptable and provide preferred time windows (UTC) so we can lock the maintenance calendar.
- Marcus / Aditya: we'll prepare an appendix with exact metric collection queries used for measuring p95/p99 and the credit calculus.

Happy to hop on a 30-min call to walk through.

Thanks,
Lauren Bishop
Runtime Lead, Serving & Performance | Redwood Inference
